vignette:
She is sixty-five now, a widow who has spent most of her working life learning how to anticipate breaches before they happen. As a cybersecurity analyst, she trusts patterns, redundancy, backup plans. She likes systems that can be hardened. What still unsettles her is that the event that rearranges her life arrives in an ordinary moment, on an ordinary road, with no warning she can detect.

Three years ago, she is driving home at dusk after a long day in the office. It has been raining on and off, the kind of slick weather she usually respects. She remembers stopping at a light, thinking about dinner, and then the impossible speed of headlights cutting across her lane. A truck has lost control coming through the intersection. She hears the violent crush of metal before she understands it is her own car being folded inward. In the seconds that follow, time stretches into fragments: the airbag exploding into her face, the taste of blood, glass on her neck, the steering wheel jammed against her chest. She cannot move her legs at first and believes, with complete certainty, that she is about to die there in the darkening rain.

What she remembers most clearly is the smell-petrol, wet upholstery, something burning-and the sound of her own breath turning shallow and animal-like. She tries to reach for her phone and cannot. Someone is shouting from outside the car not to move. She thinks of her husband, though he has already been dead for several years, and has the strange, calm thought that she might be going where he is. When paramedics finally pull her free, she is shivering uncontrollably, apologizing to them for reasons she cannot explain.

Her physical injuries heal more quickly than she expects. Bruising fades, broken ribs knit, cuts close. People around her begin to speak of how lucky she is. She nods because that is what one says. Inside, luck does not feel like the right word. She starts waking before dawn with her heart racing, certain she smells fuel in the room. Sometimes she dreams she is still pinned in the car, unable to turn her head, listening for fire. Other nights she dreams nothing at all but jolts awake soaked in sweat, already braced for impact.

At first she tells herself it will pass. She has always managed by being competent. She returns to work remotely before she is ready, laptop balanced carefully on a pillow while her chest still aches. In meetings, she finds herself drifting when colleagues speak, then snapping back with embarrassment because she has missed whole sections of conversation. She used to enjoy the puzzle of her work-tracking threats, identifying vulnerabilities, thinking three steps ahead. Now every alert sound makes her body tense. If a notification pings unexpectedly, she startles so hard she spills tea or drops her pen. She begins muting everything, then worries she will miss something critical. The old confidence she has in her judgment feels less available to her.

Driving becomes the clearest dividing line between before and after. At first she cannot get into a car unless someone else is with her. Then even as a passenger she grips the door handle and watches every intersection, silently calculating who might run a light, who is coming too fast, where they would hit. Rain is worst. Headlights reflecting on wet asphalt make her stomach clench. More than once she asks a friend to pull over so she can be sick. Eventually she starts organizing her life around not having to drive at all. Groceries are delivered. Appointments are postponed. Invitations are declined if they involve crossing town. She tells people traffic exhausts her, which is true, but not in the way they think.

Her world narrows gradually. She has no children, and since her husband died she has been used to solitude, but this is different. Solitude once felt chosen; now it feels enforced by fear. She sits in her house and monitors the environment the way she once monitored networks-scanning for anomalies, listening for danger. A car backfiring outside sends her to the floor before she can think. If she passes a wreck on the road, she loses the rest of the day. She avoids news stories about collisions, avoids certain intersections entirely, avoids dusk when she can. She is ashamed of how small her life has become and more ashamed that she cannot simply will it larger.

She speaks about the accident as if it happened both yesterday and to someone else. There are moments in session when her voice goes flat and distant, and others when a tiny detail-the hiss of rain on the windshield, the pressure of the seatbelt across her ribs-brings tears she has spent months trying not to feel. She says she is tired of living in a body that behaves as though the crash is still underway. She knows, logically, that she survived. Yet much of her day is organized around the expectation that catastrophe is seconds away, and she moves through the present as if impact has never fully ended.
